name: Checkers
intro: Learn checkers from scratch: how pieces move and jump, why captures are compulsory, crowning kings and how to win, then the shots and endgame ideas that beat stronger players.

ladder.name: Penny
ladder.blurb: Just learned the moves. Walks into jumps.

ladder.name: Mira
ladder.blurb: Steady player. Spots the simple shots.

ladder.name: The Monocle
ladder.blurb: Reads several jumps ahead. No free pieces here.

units.name: How checkers works
units.blurb: The board, moving, jumping, kings and how you win.

lessons.title: The checkers board and how to set it up
lessons.summary: How to set up a checkers board: 12 pieces each on the dark squares of the first three rows, and which way the board goes.
lessons.wrap: That’s the starting position. Next: how the pieces move.

steps.text:
Checkers (also called draughts) is played on an 8×8 board. Each player has 12 pieces, set out on the dark squares of the three rows nearest them.

Pieces only ever stand on dark squares, so half the board is never used.

Each player has a dark square in the bottom-left corner. The two middle rows start empty.

On BoardGameSite you play gold and move first. (In tournaments the darker side moves first.)
Quick check.
steps.prompt: How many pieces does each player start with?
steps.explain: 12 each, on the dark squares of the first three rows.

lessons.title: How checkers pieces move
lessons.summary: A checkers piece moves one square diagonally forward onto an empty dark square. Learn how pieces move with practice on a real board.
lessons.wrap: One step, diagonally, forwards. Next: jumping, which is how you capture.

steps.text:
A piece moves one square diagonally forward, onto an empty dark square.

Ordinary pieces (called men) can’t move backwards or sideways.
Your piece on d4 has two choices.
steps.prompt: Tap every square this piece can move to.
steps.done: c5 and e5: the two forward diagonals.

steps.text: A piece on the edge has only one forward diagonal.
steps.prompt: Tap every square this piece can move to.
steps.wrong: It can only move diagonally forward, and there’s just one way to go.
steps.done: Just b4. Edge pieces are safe from capture, but they have fewer moves.

steps.text: Your turn. Tap your piece, then the square to move it to.
steps.prompt: Move your piece forward.
steps.done: That’s a move. Then it’s your opponent’s turn.

lessons.title: How to jump and capture in checkers
lessons.summary: You capture in checkers by jumping diagonally over an enemy piece onto the empty square behind it, and if you can jump, you must.
lessons.wrap: Remember: if a jump is there, you have to take it. Next: double and triple jumps.

steps.text: You capture by jumping: hop diagonally over an enemy piece next to you, onto the empty square just behind it. The jumped piece is removed.
The black piece on d4 has an empty square behind it.
steps.prompt: Jump the black piece.
steps.wrong: Jump over the piece onto the empty square behind it.
steps.done: Captured. The black piece is off the board.

steps.text: The big rule of checkers: jumping is compulsory. If any of your pieces can jump, you must jump. You can’t make an ordinary move instead.
Your piece on c3 can jump.
steps.prompt: Can you move the piece on g3 instead?
steps.explain: No. With a jump available, every other move is off the table. Good players use this to force their opponent into bad jumps.

steps.text: Over to you.
steps.prompt: Make the move the rules require.

lessons.title: Double and triple jumps in checkers
lessons.summary: After a jump, if your piece can jump again it keeps going in the same turn. Learn multiple jumps in checkers with puzzles.
lessons.wrap: Always look for the longest chain. Next: crowning a king.

steps.text:
If, after a jump, your piece lands where it can jump again, it keeps going in the same turn. That’s a double jump, and chains can be even longer.

You must finish the whole chain: you can’t stop halfway.
Tap your piece, then each landing square in turn.
steps.prompt: Capture both black pieces in one turn.
steps.wrong: Jump to e5 first, then jump again over d6.
steps.done: Double jump! Two pieces in one move.

steps.text: Find the longest chain.
steps.prompt: Capture three pieces in one turn.
steps.wrong: Keep jumping, zig-zagging up the board: three pieces are there for the taking.

lessons.title: Kings in checkers: crowning and how they move
lessons.summary: A checkers piece that reaches the far row is crowned a king and can move and jump backwards too. Learn how kings work.
lessons.wrap: Kings are worth far more than ordinary pieces. Next: how you win.

steps.text: When one of your pieces reaches the far row, it is crowned and becomes a king.
Your piece is one step away.
steps.prompt: Move to the far row and get crowned.

steps.text: A king moves one square diagonally forwards or backwards, and can jump in all four directions too.
steps.prompt: Tap every square this king can move to.
steps.wrong: Still one square at a time, diagonally.
steps.done: Four directions. That makes kings hard to trap.

steps.text: Kings can jump backwards too.
steps.prompt: Jump the piece behind your king.
steps.done: Only a king could make that jump.

lessons.title: How to win at checkers
lessons.summary: You win at checkers by capturing all your opponent’s pieces or leaving them with no legal move. Learn both ways to win.
lessons.wrap: You know every rule of checkers. Test yourself in the rules check.

steps.text:
You win when your opponent can’t move. Usually that’s because you’ve captured all their pieces.

But it also counts if their pieces are all blocked.
Black has one piece left.
steps.prompt: Win the game.
steps.done: No black pieces left: you win!

steps.text: Black’s last piece is in the corner on h8. Its only move is to g7, where your piece stands, and your piece on f6 stops it jumping. Keep it that way.
steps.prompt: Win by leaving Black with no move.
steps.wrong: That lets Black move. Find a move that keeps the corner piece blocked.
steps.done: Black can’t move, so you win.

steps.text: And if neither side can win?
steps.prompt: Two kings each, and nobody can make progress. What happens?
options: The player with more kings wins
steps.explain: A draw. Players agree to it, or it’s declared after a long stretch with no captures.

units.name: Rules check
units.blurb: Prove you know the rules, then move on to strategy.

lessons.title: Checkers rules quiz
lessons.summary: Test your knowledge of the checkers rules: moving, compulsory jumps, multiple jumps, crowning kings and how to win.
lessons.wrap: Rules check passed. Now for the shots that win games.

steps.text: Question 1.
steps.prompt: Tap every square this piece can move to.

steps.text: Question 2.
steps.prompt: You can jump, but you’d rather make a different move. Can you?
steps.explain: No. If a jump is available, you must take one.

steps.text: Question 3.
steps.prompt: Make the best capture.
steps.wrong: Keep going after the first jump.

steps.text: Question 4.
steps.prompt: How does an ordinary piece become a king?
steps.explain: By reaching the far row. It’s crowned and can then move backwards too.

steps.text: Question 5.
steps.prompt: Win the game in one move.
steps.done: Your king jumps the last piece.

units.name: Shots and tactics
units.blurb: Use compulsory jumps to win material, and keep your own pieces safe.

lessons.title: The two-for-one shot in checkers
lessons.summary: The two-for-one shot: give up one piece to force a jump, then take two back. The most common winning tactic in checkers.
lessons.wrap: Before every move, look for a piece you can give away to set up a double jump.

steps.text:
Because jumps are compulsory, you can force your opponent to take a piece, landing exactly where you want.

Give one, take two: that’s a two-for-one shot.
Offer a piece that Black must take. Then their capturing piece becomes a stepping stone.
steps.prompt: Set up the shot: offer a piece.
steps.wrong: Look for a piece you can put next to a black piece so Black has to jump it.

lessons.title: Safe moves: don’t give pieces away
lessons.summary: Most checkers games are lost by leaving a piece where it can be jumped. Learn to check each move is safe before you make it.
lessons.wrap: Before each move, ask: can it be jumped where it lands? Next: back row defence.

steps.text:
A piece is safe if it can’t be jumped. A piece next to an enemy piece, with an empty square behind it, can be.

Edges are safe too: nothing can jump a piece on the side of the board.
The black pieces on c5 and g5 are waiting. Three of your four moves put a piece where it can be jumped.
steps.prompt: Make a move that can’t be jumped next turn.
steps.wrong: That piece could be jumped next turn: there’s an empty square behind it. Try again.
steps.done: Safe. Nothing can jump a piece on the edge.

lessons.title: Back row defence in checkers
lessons.summary: Keeping pieces on your back row stops your opponent getting kings. Learn which back row pieces to keep and why.
lessons.wrap: Guard the back row early; release it once the game opens up.

steps.text:
Your opponent gets a king by reaching your back row. Pieces on it act as guards.

A strong habit: keep the pieces on c1 and e1 at home for as long as you can. Together they cover every square a black piece could land on.
Think about crowning.
steps.prompt: Why does getting the first king matter so much?
options: Kings move backwards, so they can attack pieces from behind
Kings count as two pieces at the end
steps.explain: A king can come back and attack pieces from behind, and they have no way to escape.

units.name: Endgames
units.blurb: Racing for kings and finishing a game you’re winning.

lessons.title: Racing to crown a king
lessons.summary: In checkers endgames, the first player to crown a king usually wins. Learn to count the race and pick the right piece to run.
lessons.wrap: Count moves to the far row before you start running.

steps.text: With only a few pieces left, the first king usually decides the game. Count how many moves each piece needs to reach the far row.
Your piece on f4 needs 4 moves to crown; the one on b2 needs 6.
steps.prompt: Which piece should run?
options: The piece on f4: it’s closer
The piece on b2: it’s further from danger
steps.explain: The closer piece, as long as it can get past safely. Count the race: fewer moves to the crown wins it.

steps.text: The black piece on d6 can jump anything that lands on e5. Run around it.
steps.prompt: Move the runner forward safely.
steps.wrong: That square can be jumped, or slows you down. Go around the black piece.
steps.done: Safe, and on the way to the crown.

lessons.title: Trapping pieces in checkers
lessons.summary: You can win a checkers piece without jumping it by blocking it until it’s forced into a losing move. Learn to trap pieces on the edge.
lessons.wrap: Pieces on the edge and in corners are easiest to trap. That completes the Checkers path: time for the ladder.

steps.text: Pieces don’t have to be jumped to be lost. If a piece’s only moves walk into a jump, it’s trapped.
Black’s piece on a5 can only move to b4, and your piece is already there, backed up by c3 so it can’t be jumped. You have to move something, though.
steps.prompt: Make a move that leaves Black stuck.
steps.wrong: That frees the black piece. Keep b4 and c3 where they are and move your spare piece.
steps.done: Trapped: Black has no move, so you win.
